why/gather: Self-attention lets every token gather from the others. In the sentence, cats like fish, fish comes out as a blend of their values: half from cats, a quarter from like, and a quarter from itself.
why/alone: A blend moves information between tokens. To work on what it gathered, each token then goes through a small network on its own: the two-layer network, with a ReLU between its layers.
why/mlp: This network is called an MLP, for multilayer perceptron: neurons in layers, named after Rosenblatt's perceptron, though they bend with a ReLU rather than a step.
why/paper: In 2017, Ashish Vaswani and colleagues built a translation model around this pair: attention, then one MLP, applied to each token separately and identically. They called it the Transformer.
why/stack: One attention and one MLP make a block, and the model stacks identical blocks, six in the paper. So a block must hand back what it takes in: T tokens, each a vector of d numbers.
parts/path: Now the block as it is really built. Draw a token's path straight down through it, from the input, x, to the output.
parts/branch: Attention sits on a branch beside the path. The branch first runs layer norm, so attention reads every token on the same scale, then multi-head attention.
parts/add: Its output is added back onto the path: a residual connection, x plus attention of layer norm of x. So the branch only has to learn a change to x.
parts/grid: Inside, attention builds a T by T grid of weights, but it hands back one vector of d numbers per token: the shape of x. That is what lets the add line up.
parts/mlp: Then a second branch, built the same way: layer norm, the MLP, and another add.
parts/width: The MLP widens each token to four d numbers, applies the ReLU there, and brings it back down to d. In the paper, d was five hundred twelve, so the middle was two thousand and forty eight wide.
parts/out: Out comes T by d, the shape that went in, ready for the next block.
norms/post: The 2017 paper put each layer norm somewhere else: after its add, right on the path.
norms/road: Then the path itself runs through a norm in every block, and so does every gradient flowing back along it.
norms/xiong: In 2020, Ruibin Xiong and colleagues showed what that costs. With the norms on the path, the gradients near the output start out large, so training has to begin with a small step size and raise it slowly.
norms/pre: Move each norm to the start of its branch, and the path is bare: from input to output, only adds, like a residual network's shortcut. This is the pre-norm block.
norms/calm: There, they found, the gradients start out well behaved, and pre-norm blocks trained well with no slow start.
flow/x: Follow one token through, with d of two, so it is an arrow on a page. It enters as one and two.
flow/a: The attention branch hands back a change: zero point five and minus one. Added tip to tail, the arrow now ends at one point five and one.
flow/m: The MLP branch reads that sum, normalized, and hands back minus zero point five and two. Added on, the arrow ends at one and three: the block's output.
flow/path: The token is never replaced, only nudged, once by each branch, while x itself runs straight through both adds.
